title: Andrew Aversa - The End of Permadeath
speaker: Andrew Aversa
summary: Andrew Aversa (developer of Tangledeep) examines optional permadeath: how many roguelikes offer it, how the way the option is presented sets player expectations, and how the default mode changes what content developers must build. He argues permadeath is a promise that the early game will be varied and replayable and that story cannot be front-loaded, while no-permadeath promises a rich endgame and payoff. Designing equally for both is hard on small budgets, and player reviews show mismatched expectations. He surveys alternatives (lives, wizard mode, save points) and urges developers to ask whether they can keep the promise permadeath makes.

insights.claim: Optional permadeath is better defined as any mode where dying does not necessarily cost all progress, spanning a spectrum rather than an on/off switch.
insights.detail: Aversa includes partial losses (keep some things, lose weapons or experience), lives, saves, rewinds and checkpoints where a dead-end timeline is lost but an earlier point remains. He notes many traditional and new roguelikes offer it, citing Stoneshard as a major recent hit where permadeath is optional and, he believes, not the default.
insights.quote: Any mode or option where the player is not necessarily doomed to lose all their progress upon dying

insights.claim: The default mode and how a permadeath option is presented strongly shape how players perceive and play a roguelike, before any balance considerations.
insights.detail: Aversa cites opt-in versus opt-out organ donation studies, where defaults change behaviour enormously in otherwise similar populations. The title screen and character creation already set the stage for how people will play.
insights.quote: How we define the default experience of a game as developers is monumentally important and affects how the game is perceived

insights.claim: Permadeath options can be presented on a scale from no option, preselected toggle, nestled submenu, hidden, to equal selection, each sending a different message about intended play.
insights.detail: No in-game option is the strongest statement of intent; a preselected toggle is a big nudge; nestling it in a submenu downplays it; hidden (only via file editing) says you cannot do this. Listing options with none highlighted is the most equitable and likely gets roughly even evaluation.
insights.quote: This is the strongest statement we can make as a developer to say this is the way you play our game

insights.claim: Mode labels communicate developer judgment: Wolfenstein and Doom mock easy modes, Celeste gates assist options behind a gentle warning, and ADOM lists modes equitably.
insights.detail: Aversa contrasts labels that tell players they are weak with story modes that say no less of you. Celeste offers invincibility but only after a screen recommending playing as intended first. ADOM presents standard and hard ahead of roguelike mode, which he finds equitable, though he saw it later tell a standard-mode player they could progress to the 'real' classic mode.
insights.quote: Both wolfenstein and doom show everything but the way they are labeled tells the player this isn't the real mode

insights.claim: Default permadeath promises that early content will be seen repeatedly, so developers must invest heavily in early-game variety in starts, monsters, locations and character creation.
insights.detail: Aversa graphs time in a run against content: permadeath produces a pyramid wide at the bottom. If players expecting permadeath get the same five floors and layouts, they get bored and may leave negative reviews.
insights.quote: You are making a promise to the player that you are going to die and so we going to make, as developers, a wide variety of content

insights.claim: A permadeath roguelike cannot front-load an intrusive cinematic story because repeated early-game play makes any opening sequence stale.
insights.detail: Aversa contrasts JRPG or cinematic games with five-minute intros before control. If players die often and replay the beginning, even the best opening becomes stale very quickly.
insights.quote: if you are going to be playing this early game repeatedly then we can't really make an intrusive story

insights.claim: Without permadeath, players expect to reach the end, so the final boss, endgame options, gear progression and story payoff must deliver.
insights.detail: Players breeze into midgame and expect to beat the game; they want hidden bosses, a gear treadmill of upgrades in loot-driven games, and a story payoff. Aversa cites Diablo III being maligned when its story did not meet expectations in a non-permadeath game.
insights.quote: That brings up player expectations and the final boss better be good

insights.claim: Designing equally for permadeath and non-permadeath modes is hard on small budgets, and hazards acceptable without permadeath feel unfair with it.
insights.detail: Developers must make concessions in where they invest effort. A monster hitting half your HP or an invisible trap may be fine with saves but provokes 'this is unfair, I lost my progress' reviews from permadeath players if the developer did not anticipate that alignment.
insights.quote: Something that may be perfectly acceptable in a non-permadeath mode for oh, this monster hits half your HP and an invisible trap

insights.claim: Player reviews of traditional roguelikes show opposite reactions to the same permadeath structures, from hating the early-game slog to finding the endgame thin.
insights.detail: One reviewer loved a game without permadeath but found replaying the early game a slog with it on; another resented 13 hours to reach a great endgame; another said fun happens in the first half and gear and strategy converge by the end. Aversa suggests different design or option presentation might have set different expectations.
insights.quote: Permadeath on is fun until you realize you have to go through the early game slog again to get back to where you were

insights.claim: A lives system is a compromise that lets designers push fairness limits and offer new rewards while not wiping all progress on one death.
insights.detail: Aversa lists permadeath-off as the simplest alternative (die and lose resources), lives as a compromise giving room for 'a few unfair things', and wizard mode as an explicit no-guarantees option.
insights.quote: It gives the designer a lot more room to say yes, we can do a few unfair things and push the limits

insights.claim: Save-anywhere or checkpoint saves are not necessarily easier than permadeath because a player can save into an unrecoverable state.
insights.detail: Deep in a dungeon without enough healing, a saved game can be doomed, which feels like an impossible puzzle, like a door locking until you starve, rather than a heroic death. Aversa places it between no permadeath and default permadeath.
insights.quote: this is not necessarily easier than permadeath off or lives because you could potentially save the game in a situation where you cannot recover

insights.claim: Developers should include permadeath only if they can fulfil its promise of a fun, varied early game without a heavy opening story; otherwise it should not be the default.
insights.detail: Aversa asks whether you are ready to promise the early game will be fun and character creation varied. If the experience you want to promise is epic late-game battles, like fighting dragons on a neutron star, players should reach it sooner, so permadeath maybe should not be the default.
insights.quote: we should think about why we are including permadeath in the game and if we are willing to fulfill the promise

insights.claim: Meta-progression can bridge permadeath tension, but it frustrates when it feels like required dying and excites when it offers new options like starting locations.
insights.detail: In Q&A Aversa says meta-progress keeps the feeling of danger without scaring players off, but implementations can go either way: 'I have to die to build up my character' versus 'even if I die I get to pick another starting location'.
insights.quote: I think there is a lot of implementations of meta progress that can make people feel frustrated like I have to die to build up my character

insights.claim: Run length changes how harsh permanent consequences feel: losing a 10-15 hour run hurts far more than a coffee-break roguelike or board game.
insights.detail: In Q&A on comparisons to board games where mistakes matter, Aversa says it is about framing expectations, and the average session length changes how people feel about spikes that take 80% of their health.
insights.quote: the length of the play session can also change a little bit the framing from the developer and the player
